prompt.context: Our client is the Dean of Kellogg School of Management. She has hired you to advise her on an idea which struck her during the previous week – to consider starting a satellite campus of Kellogg in India.
prompt.question: Should Kellogg enter the Indian market by starting a satellite campus? The Dean wants the satellite campus to breakeven in 4 years.

clarifying_info.q: Why is the Dean considering India?
clarifying_info.a: India is one of the fastest-growing economies with a huge demand for business education, both domestically and for students travelling abroad. Dean Sally believes it would help Kellogg move to the Top 3.

clarifying_info.q: What is the target breakeven timeline?
clarifying_info.a: The Dean wants the satellite campus to breakeven in 4 years.

clarifying_info.q: Will there be any compromise on student quality?
clarifying_info.a: No. The quality of students and the selection procedure would be comparable to the current procedure; there will be no compromise on the quality of applicants to increase revenue.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the local competitors in India?
clarifying_info.a: India has its own top-tier business schools such as the 7 Indian Institutes of Management (IIM) and the Indian School of Business (ISB). ISB has a tie-up with Kellogg for its pedagogy.

clarifying_info.q: How do Indian B-schools select students?
clarifying_info.a: IIMs admit via the Common Admission Test (CAT). ISB admits candidates based on GMAT.

clarifying_info.q: What does MBA education cost in India vs. Kellogg?
clarifying_info.a: It costs a student about $20,000 per year for an MBA in India, compared to about $70,000 at Kellogg. Indian schools don't offer many scholarships but banks offer generous educational loans for top MBA schools.
Only the 2-year MBA program to start with.

exhibits.title: B-Schools in India
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the IIMs and ISB across program description and cost incurred by the student.
exhibits.data: IIMs: CAT has 500,000 applications/year; top 6% shortlisted for interview; 5 candidates interviewed per slot; 85% of admitted candidates join an IIM; ISB: 70% of admitted students matriculate each year between two campuses for a total class size of 1,400; Cost: INR 1,200,000 per year (all expenses included); conversion rate 1 USD = 60 INR; Kellogg Evanston cost assumed $70,000 per annum

exhibits.title: Number of Admitted Students
exhibits.shows: A table showing the expected number of new students to be admitted each year at the Kellogg India campus across four years.

exhibits.title: Intake and Cost Structure
exhibits.shows: A table of total variable costs per year and the initial (Year 0) fixed costs for the Kellogg India campus.
exhibits.data: Variable costs: Year 1 $30M, Year 2 $30M, Year 3 $30M, Year 4 $20M; Initial cost (Year 0): Land acquisition and campus setup $100M, Support infrastructure $50M, Total $150M

framework: Market attractiveness: size and growth of Indian MBA market, competitive landscape (IIMs, ISB), regulatory environment
Strategic fit: alignment with Kellogg brand, ranking impact, cannibalisation of existing Indian student intake at Evanston
Quantitative analysis: market sizing (bottom-up), revenue build (fee × students), cost structure (fixed + variable), breakeven/NPV analysis
Qualitative factors: brand dilution risk, job prospects and employer perception, ROI for students, faculty/infrastructure support from parent campus

questions.prompt: Estimate the total addressable market of high-quality MBA students in India each year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should attempt a bottom-up approach using IIM and ISB data from Exhibit A. IIM pipeline: 500,000 CAT applications → top 6% shortlisted = 30,000 → 1 in 5 accepted = 6,000 → 85% matriculate ≈ 5,100 (but guide uses accepted count of 6,000 as the pool). ISB pipeline: 1,400 total class size across two campuses, 70% matriculation rate implied → admitted pool ≈ 2,000. Total addressable market ≈ 6,000 (IIM pool) + 2,000 (ISB pool) = 8,000 prospective students per year. A top-down approach is acceptable but becomes heavily assumption-dependent.

math.setup: IIM: 500,000 applications × 6% shortlisted = 30,000; 30,000 × (1/5) accepted = 6,000. ISB: class size 1,400 / 70% matriculation = 2,000 admitted. TAM = 6,000 + 2,000.
math.answer: Total addressable market ≈ 8,000 high-quality MBA students per year in India

questions.prompt: What fee should Kellogg India charge, and what is the annual revenue in each of the four years?
questions.guidance: Fee should sit between the Indian market rate ($20,000/yr) and Kellogg Evanston ($70,000/yr). A value around $50,000/yr is reasonable; challenge candidates who go too low or too high. Revenue = new cohort fee + continuing cohort fee from prior year (2-year program). Use student numbers from Exhibit B.

math.setup: Fee = $50,000/yr. Revenue each year = (new students admitted that year × $50,000) + (students admitted previous year × $50,000, i.e., their second year). Y1: only first-year cohort. Y2+: two cohorts paying simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Build the cost structure and determine whether the campus breaks even within 4 years.
questions.guidance: Year 0 fixed costs from Exhibit C: $150M (land/campus $100M + support infrastructure $50M). Variable costs from Exhibit C: Y1 $30M, Y2 $30M, Y3 $30M, Y4 $20M. Profit each year = Revenue – Variable cost. Cumulative profit must recover $150M initial investment. Candidate should ask for a discount rate; there is none given, so proceed without discounting. By Y4 cumulative net = –$150M + $0 + $30M + $45M + $70M = –$5M. Does not quite break even by Y4. A strong candidate notes the miss is only $5M, revenues are rising to $90M in Y4 while costs are falling to $20M, so breakeven occurs in the first month of Y5.

math.setup: Cumulative profit = sum of annual profits net of $150M initial outlay. Annual profit = Revenue – Variable cost.
steps: Breakeven not achieved in Y4; miss = $5M. Given trajectory, breakeven in early Y5.
math.answer: Cumulative shortfall at end of Y4 = –$5M; campus breaks even very early in Year 5, just missing the 4-year target.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors should be evaluated before recommending whether Kellogg should open a satellite campus in India?

categories.name: Brand impact
ideas: No top US B-school (except INSEAD) has successfully launched a satellite campus in India – brand dilution risk is real
Global employers may not view Kellogg India MBA on par with Kellogg Evanston, reducing ROI for graduates
Satellite campus may dilute Kellogg's selectivity perception and reputation

categories.name: Rankings
ideas: Impact on diversity metric – a more India-heavy class could reduce diversity scores
International presence metric may improve due to Asian footprint
Average salary of Indian graduates (adjusted for Indian PPP) reported globally could depress Kellogg's salary ranking

categories.name: Cannibalisation
ideas: Kellogg Evanston currently admits 50–60 Indian students per year; a local campus could reduce these applications
High-quality applicants from other Asian countries might redirect to Kellogg India instead of Evanston

categories.name: Student ROI
ideas: Fee charged ($50,000/yr) is 2.5× the Indian market rate; students must see commensurate salary uplift
Job placement rates and employer willingness to hire Kellogg India graduates need to be verified

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Faculty sourcing and quality – reliance on parent campus for pedagogical support is critical
Infrastructure and campus quality must match Kellogg standards
Regulatory and licensing requirements from the Indian government

categories.name: Financial
ideas: $150M initial investment while Kellogg Evanston is also building a new facility raises fundraising strain
Potential for additional revenue from executive education, corporate training, and supporting programs
Indian government subsidies or partnerships could lower initial investment

recommendation: From a financial standpoint the satellite campus is viable: it breaks even in early Year 5 (missing the 4-year target by only ~$5M) with revenues growing to $90M and variable costs declining to $20M in Year 4.
However, a final go/no-go decision should not be made until the impact on Brand Kellogg, rankings, and cannibalisation of the Evanston intake is studied in detail.
risks: Brand dilution if global employers and applicants perceive Kellogg India as a lower-tier offering
Negative ranking impact from Indian graduate salary data reported globally
Cannibalisation of existing Indian and Asian student applications to Evanston
50% jump in admitted cohort from Year 2 to Year 3 is aggressive and may not be achievable
$150M capital requirement coincides with Kellogg's new Evanston building, creating fundraising pressure
next_steps: Hire a brand agency to quantify the impact of a satellite campus on Brand Kellogg
Secure funding of $150M through fundraising and explore Indian government subsidies
Identify potential academic and corporate partners for faculty, infrastructure, and student recruitment
Begin discussions with the Indian government on land, licenses, and potential incentives
Develop additional revenue streams (executive education, corporate training) to improve financial robustness
